hook: Hubert Dreyfus was born in Terre Haute, Indiana, in 1929 and studied philosophy at Harvard, earning his doctorate in 1964. While teaching at MIT in the early 1960s, he was asked by the RAND Corporation to evaluate the prospects of artificial intelligence and concluded, against the confident predictions of the field's founders, that AI's symbolic, rule-based approach could not capture the embodied, skillful coping that underlies everyday human intelligence. He expanded this critique into the 1972 book What Computers Can't Do: A Critique of Artificial Reason, drawing on the phenomenology of Martin Heidegger and Maurice Merleau-Ponty to argue that meaning and skill arise from a body acting in a world, not from symbols manipulated in a mind. He moved to the University of California, Berkeley, in 1968, where he taught for the rest of his career and became one of the most influential interpreters of Heidegger in America. He updated his argument in What Computers Still Can't Do (1992) as the field shifted toward neural networks, and his claim that intelligence depends on a body skillfully coping with a world anticipated the embodied and situated approaches that later reshaped robotics and AI.
name: Hubert Dreyfus

quote.text: They said they could program computers to be intelligent like people. I really wanted to know, could they do it?
quote.context: 2005 interview, as quoted in his obituary in Communications of the ACM (2017)

moniker: Philosopher who challenged AI with phenomenology

quick_facts: Born in Terre Haute, Indiana, in 1929, and earned his Ph.D. in philosophy from Harvard in 1964
Evaluated artificial intelligence research for the RAND Corporation while teaching at MIT in the early 1960s
Published What Computers Can't Do: A Critique of Artificial Reason in 1972
Drew on Martin Heidegger and Maurice Merleau-Ponty to argue that embodied, skillful coping underlies human intelligence
Taught philosophy at the University of California, Berkeley, from 1968 until his death in 2017
Updated his critique in What Computers Still Can't Do (1992)

achievements.title: What Computers Can't Do: A Critique of Artificial Reason (1972)
achievements.impact: Argued from phenomenology that symbolic AI could not reproduce the embodied, situated skill that underlies ordinary human intelligence, a critique that forced AI researchers to confront the limits of rule-based reasoning.

achievements.title: RAND Corporation report on artificial intelligence (1965)
achievements.impact: One of the earliest outside assessments of AI research, questioning the field's founding assumptions years before its first widely acknowledged setbacks.

achievements.title: What Computers Still Can't Do (1992)
achievements.impact: Extended his critique to connectionist and neural-network approaches, arguing embodiment, not just different computation, was still missing.

achievements.title: Interpretation of Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty for English-language philosophy
achievements.impact: Made continental phenomenology accessible and applicable to debates in cognitive science and AI, influencing embodied and situated approaches to robotics.
